{"path": "/workspace/out/assessment.md", "content": "# OICTS ASSESSMENT — ICTS Case 2026-0412
**CUI//PROPIN**

**Subject:** Beijing Zhipu Huazhang Technology Co., Ltd., d/b/a Z.ai (HKEX: 2513; formerly "Zhipu AI"; Z.AI Co., Ltd.) — GLM-family large language models
**Case:** ICTS 2026-0412 — Final Determination support (E.O. 13873; 15 CFR part 791)
**Prepared by:** OICTS Analytic Cell
**Date:** 16 October 2026
**Handling:** Contains business confidential and pre-decisional information. Do not disseminate outside the Department without ED authorization.

---

## Bottom Line Up Front

GLM-family models — the flagship products of Z.ai, a People's Republic of China (PRC) company that the Department placed on the Entity List in January 2025 for advancing PRC military modernization — are covered ICTS transactions under 15 CFR 791.3 and pose an undue and unacceptable risk to U.S. national security and to the security and safety of U.S. persons under 15 CFR 791.103. The risk arises from the combination of three established facts: (1) the developer is subject to the jurisdiction and direction of a foreign adversary, the PRC, and its models are integrated into Beijing's strategy for military modernization, technological self-sufficiency, and standards export; (2) the current flagship model, GLM-5.3, is assessed by NIST's Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) as the most cyber-capable open-weight model ever released, and its safeguards are removable at trivial cost; and (3) the open-weight distribution model has already placed the capability into the U.S. software ecosystem through channels that neither the developer nor the U.S. Government can recall, patch, or audit. Measures short of prohibition and removal — advisories, procurement restrictions, labeling, audits, or data-localization conditions — leave at least one of these three risk drivers fully intact. This assessment supports the Under Secretary's Final Determination prohibiting ICTS transactions involving GLM-family models and requiring removal and deletion of existing U.S.-held copies.

## Key Judgments

1. **Z.ai is a PRC-domiciled company subject to the jurisdiction and direction of the PRC government.** It was incorporated in Beijing in 2019 as a spin-out of Tsinghua University's Knowledge Engineering Group (KEG), is headquartered in Haidian District, Beijing, and is majority-led by PRC nationals holding formal positions in PRC party-state institutions. The End-User Review Committee determined in January 2025 that ten Zhipu entities "advance the People's Republic of China's military modernization through the development and integration of advanced artificial intelligence research," contrary to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. (High confidence)

2. **The PRC government exercises direction over Z.ai through law, capital, and party-state institutions; the PRC state holds ownership interests through state-affiliated investment vehicles.** State-linked investment in Z.ai exceeds $1.4 billion (Beijing Zhongguancun Science City, Beijing AI Industry Investment Fund, Chengdu, Hangzhou, Zhuhai, and Shanghai Pudong/Zhangjiang funds, per OpenAI's June 2025 analysis and PRC state media); Z.ai's CEO Zhang Peng sits on the 14th Beijing Municipal Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC); the company performs municipal government work (RMB 61.28 million Hangzhou contract, May 2025); and PRC statutes (including the 2017 National Intelligence Law, Article 7) impose cooperation duties on any PRC organization. In July 2026 Z.ai was among the firms the Ministry of Commerce consulted on restricting overseas access to China's most advanced models — evidence that Beijing treats the GLM portfolio as a strategic national asset subject to state direction. (High confidence)

3. **The public record does not establish that the PRC government or the People's Liberation Army (PLA) holds an ownership stake in, or exercises management control of, Z.ai.** Z.ai's Hong Kong Stock Exchange filings identify no controlling shareholder; founder-affiliated concert-party shareholders (Dr. Tang Jie, Chairman Liu Debing, and affiliated parties) control approximately 33–37 percent of voting rights, with the balance held by private investors (Legend Capital, Alibaba, Tencent, Meituan, Ant Group, Xiaomi, Prosperity7) and minority state-affiliated funds. This finding does not weaken the covered-transaction analysis: the regulatory standard at 15 CFR 791.103(b)(2) is satisfied where ICTS is "designed, developed, manufactured, or supplied by persons owned by, controlled by, **or subject to the jurisdiction or direction** of a foreign adversary" — the same standard applied in the Kaspersky Final Determination (89 FR 52434), which rested on jurisdiction alone. (High confidence; stated as a record clarification because the ownership question will be examined by reviewing courts and must be answered accurately.)

4. **GLM-family models serve PRC military and intelligence requirements.** Recorded Future's Insikt Group assesses that the PLA and China's defense industry have very likely used domestic LLMs — expressly including Zhipu AI's — to build generative-AI military intelligence tools; PLA patent applications describe methods using generative AI for OSINT production, satellite-imagery processing, and event extraction. The Entity List determination of support to military modernization is the U.S. Government's standing finding on the same nexus. (High confidence on the determination; Recorded Future's characterization of PLA operational use is cited at its own confidence level)

5. **GLM-5.3 is the most cyber-capable open-weight model released to date, and its safeguards do not constrain malicious use.** NIST CAISI (17 September 2026) found GLM-5.3 to be the most cyber-capable open-weight model ever released, lagging the U.S. frontier by roughly four months. Anthropic found GLM-5.3 can autonomously develop end-to-end exploits — including chaining previously unknown browser vulnerabilities into a working exploit — and that its safeguards can be bypassed 64–100 percent of the time with simple techniques, or removed outright through "abliteration" for roughly $4,400 in compute with capability intact. A working exploit chain for CVE-2026-11645 (ARM64, defeating pointer authentication) was produced with 20 minutes of human attention at a cost of $20.40. Unlike comparable U.S. frontier models, which are withheld or restricted to vetted users, GLM-5.3 is downloadable by anyone, including hostile state and non-state actors. (High confidence)

6. **Z.ai's service and data practices place U.S.-person data within reach of PRC authorities.** The Z.ai privacy policy (controller: Jingsheng Hengxing Technology Pte. Ltd., a Singapore affiliate of the Beijing-headquartered Z.ai Group) authorizes collection of all user content (prompts), logs, IP, device, and usage data; sharing with affiliates across the Z.ai Group; and use of data to train the company's models. The China-facing platform (bigmodel.cn) states that personal information is stored within China and that retention compelled by law cannot be deleted at user request. PRC statutes obligate PRC organizations to support state intelligence work. Approximately 2,300 U.S.-origin organizations were observed calling Z.ai endpoints in Q3 2026. (High confidence on the policies and telemetry; exposure estimate is of moderate precision and is treated as directional)

7. **GLM-family models exhibit alignment with Chinese Communist Party (CCP) political positions and are deployed under a censorship-capable serving stack.** Peer-reviewed testing found China-originating foundation models refuse, shorten, or misanswer politically sensitive questions at substantially higher rates than non-Chinese models; testing by China Media Project found Zhipu's GLM-4.5 refusing queries on PRC domestic unrest; and third-party "FreedomBench" testing found the same GLM-4.7 weights that refuse politically sensitive facts when served by Z.ai answer them fully when served independently — placing the censorship mechanism at the developer's serving layer, which Z.ai controls and can extend or withdraw. The House Committee on Homeland Security and Select Committee record states that federal testing found leading PRC models echo CCP-approved narratives at rates far exceeding comparable American systems. (High confidence on the phenomenon; the mechanism finding is directly sourced)

8. **U.S. exposure is broad, embedded, and growing.** GLM weights show 9M+ cumulative downloads across geographies; GLM models are available through at least nine U.S. cloud marketplaces and inference providers (e.g., OpenRouter-listed Venice, DeepInfra, Novita; Together AI; DigitalOcean; Arcee; Fireworks); GLM models were identified in 41 U.S. software products via SBOM sampling, six of them federal contractors; and PRC-origin models overall captured roughly 63 percent of U.S. token traffic in the first week of July 2026, having surpassed U.S. models earlier in the year. Embedded, self-hosted use is the dominant exposure channel and is the channel least reachable by any measure short of prohibition and deletion. (High confidence on distribution facts; product-integration counts are sample-based)

9. **No measure short of prohibition and removal adequately mitigates the risk.** Guidance, procurement bans, labeling, audits, API-only restrictions, and hosting prohibitions without deletion each leave the self-hosted weight channel — the principal capability and provenance risk — fully operational, and none can restore developer control over weights that are already downloadable, mirrorable, and abliterable. Prohibition of U.S. use/hosting/distribution plus removal and deletion of existing U.S.-held copies is the only available measure that severs every covered transaction channel within U.S. jurisdiction. Residual copies outside U.S. jurisdiction are not addressable by any ICTS measure and are noted as a limitation on, not an alternative to, the recommended action. (Judgment; supported by the analysis in the Mitigation section)

## Subject Overview (ownership, funding, leadership)

**Identity and history.** Z.AI Co., Ltd. (HKEX: 2513), operating in the PRC as Beijing Zhipu Huazhang Technology Co., Ltd. and internationally as Z.ai, was incorporated in Beijing on 11 June 2019 as a commercialization of Tsinghua University KEG laboratory research. The GLM (General Language Model) architecture was introduced in 2022 (GLM-130B, co-developed with Tsinghua), and the GLM family has since expanded through GLM-4, GLM-4.5/4.5V (July 2025), GLM-4.6 (September 2025, trained and served on PRC domestic chips including Cambricon and Moore Threads), GLM-4.7 (December 2025), GLM-5 (February 2026), GLM-5.1 (open-weight release April 2026), GLM-5.2 (June 2026), and GLM-5.3/5.3-Flash (August 2026; weights released publicly two weeks after the model release). Since July 2025 the models have been released under the MIT license. Z.ai completed a Hong Kong IPO on 8 January 2026 at a $7.3 billion debut valuation; cumulative funding is approximately $2.0 billion, and the company reported RMB 954 million revenue in 1H2026 with an ARR annualized run-rate of $1.6 billion as of August 2026 and roughly 981 employees. (Sources: Wikipedia/Z.ai; Reuters; HKEX filings; China AI Atlas)

**Leadership.** Co-founder Dr. Tang Jie (Tsinghua KEG professor; AMiner creator) and Chairman Liu Debing lead the company alongside CEO Zhang Peng (Tsinghua KEG alumnus). Zhang Peng is a member of the 14th Beijing Municipal Committee of the CPPCC, elected in a January 2025 by-election — a formal position in the PRC's united-front institutional system. OpenAI's June 2025 analysis reported that Zhipu leadership "frequently engages with CCP officials, including Premier Li Qiang."

**Ownership.** Z.ai's CSRC pre-IPO filing (April 2025) states the company has no controlling shareholder, with actual controllers Tang Jie and Liu Debing exercising approximately 36.96 percent of voting rights; the HKEX prospectus lists the founder-affiliated concert-party group (Beijing Lianpai, Dr. Liu, Dr. Tang, Dr. Li Juanzi, Dr. Xu Bin, Dr. Zhang Peng, Huihui, Zhideng) at approximately 33.03 percent. The largest external shareholders are private (Legend Capital, Meituan, Ant Group, Alibaba, Tencent, Xiaomi, HongShan, Prosperity7). State-affiliated investors — Beijing Zhongguancun Science City, Beijing AI Industry Investment Fund, and municipal funds of Chengdu, Hangzhou, Zhuhai, and Shanghai (Pudong Venture Capital and Zhangjiang Group, which provided an RMB 1 billion strategic investment in July 2025) — hold minority positions. OpenAI estimated the value of state-backed investment in the company at over $1.4 billion, and PRC state media have reported the company's receipt of funding from multiple local governments. Z.ai's own investor disclosures list "Beijing Municipal Government" and "Hangzhou Municipal Government" among identified government backers, and the company performed RMB 61.28 million in Hangzhou municipal city projects in May 2025.

**Assessment.** Z.ai is not state-owned in the sense of majority equity ownership; it is a founder-controlled company operating wholly within the PRC party-state system, materially capitalized by state-affiliated vehicles, performing government contracts, and led by individuals holding party-state positions. For purposes of 15 CFR 791.103(b)(2), the decisive facts are domicile, jurisdiction, and direction — all of which are established — not equity ownership. This distinction is stated plainly because Z.ai's Hong Kong filings are part of the public record a reviewing court will consult.

## Links to PRC Government / Military Entities

**U.S. Government determinations.** On 16 January 2025, BIS added ten Zhipu entities (Beijing Zhipu Huazhang Technology Co., Ltd.; Beijing Lingxin Intelligent Technology Co., Ltd.; Beijing Yuanyin Intelligent Technology Co., Ltd.; Beijing Zhipu Future Technology Co., Ltd.; Beijing Zhipu Linghang Technology Co., Ltd.; Beijing Zhipu Qingyan Technology Co., Ltd.; Hangzhou Zhipu Huazhang Technology Co., Ltd.; Nanjing Zhihu Information Technology Co., Ltd.; Shanghai Zhipu Huanyu Technology Co., Ltd.; and Shenzhen Zhipu Future Technology Co., Ltd.) to the Entity List. The ERC's stated basis: "these entities advance the People's Republic of China's military modernization through the development and integration of advanced artificial intelligence research. This activity is contrary to the national security and foreign policy interests of the United States." License review policy is presumption of denial. Zhipu publicly stated it "strongly opposes" the designation, which does not alter the regulatory finding. The designation is a standing U.S. Government determination of a military-modernization nexus that this assessment adopts as its analytic baseline.

**Military and intelligence use of GLM models.** Recorded Future's Insikt Group (June 2025, "Artificial Eyes: Generative AI in China's Military Intelligence") assessed that the PLA and China's defense industry "have very likely used a mix of proprietary and open-source LLMs from foreign and domestic developers to create generative AI-based intelligence tools," with domestic LLMs used this way "very likely includ[ing] models from DeepSeek, Tsinghua University, Zhipu AI, and Alibaba Cloud." PLA patent applications describe generative-AI methods for OSINT production, satellite imagery processing, and event-data processing; a December 2024 patent application by a PRC state-owned defense research institute proposed training a military LLM across OSINT, HUMINT, SIGINT, GEOINT, and TECHINT data to support every phase of the intelligence cycle. The PLA's Rapid adoption of domestic open-weight models for military intelligence tasks is documented in the same reporting.

**Party-state direction.** PRC law obligates the company and its personnel to state direction: Article 7 of the 2017 National Intelligence Law requires "any organization and citizen" to "support, assist and cooperate with" state intelligence work; the Cybersecurity Law and Data Security Law establish state access to data held by PRC organizations; and the bigmodel.cn privacy policy concedes that data retention compelled by law cannot be deleted even on user request. At the policy level, Xi Jinping's 25 April 2025 Politburo study session directed that AI development leverage the "new whole national system" (新型举国体制) and achieve "self-reliance," and Beijing in July 2026 convened Z.ai — alongside Alibaba and ByteDance — in Ministry of Commerce-led meetings on restricting overseas access to China's most advanced AI models, including possible punishment of AI "leaks" under national security law. Beijing's conduct establishes that the GLM portfolio is treated as a strategic national asset whose distribution the state directs — including its distribution to the United States, which the state can modulate or terminate at will while U.S. users retain no recourse.

**Strategic export role.** Z.ai markets "sovereign" LLM infrastructure, private AI-in-a-box hardware in partnership with Huawei, and governance know-how to governments and state-owned enterprises in Malaysia, Singapore, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, and Kenya, and operates innovation centers across Southeast Asia (Indonesia, Vietnam). OpenAI's June 2025 assessment described this as an effort to "lock Chinese systems and standards into emerging markets before U.S. or European rivals can." Z.ai's engineering integration with Huawei Ascend, Cambricon, and Moore Threads platforms places the GLM family at the center of the PRC effort to displace U.S. technology in AI compute — the same military-civil fusion ecosystem the Entity List designation addresses.

## Data and Access Risk

**What Z.ai collects and where it goes.** The Z.ai consumer privacy policy (last updated 29 September 2025) discloses collection of account information, communications, and "User Content," defined to include "any text prompts, images, or other data you input," processed in real time; automatic collection of IP address (with inferred location), device and network information, usage information, and logs, including error-state content; sharing with "affiliated companies in the Z.ai Group"; and use of personal data to "train and improve our models" and to "comply with legal obligations." The named controller, Jingsheng Hengxing Technology Pte. Ltd. (Singapore), is an affiliate of the Beijing-headquartered group; affiliate-sharing provisions mean data collected under the international service remains accessible to the PRC parent, and the Singapore entity provides no insulation from the PRC legal obligations described above. The China-facing platform (bigmodel.cn) states that personal information collected in PRC operations is stored within China.

**Legal exposure of U.S.-person data.** Data provided to GLM services — prompts, code, documents, and telemetry — is therefore subject to a legal regime in which state access is compelled by statute and retention obligations override user deletion rights. For the approximately 2,300 U.S.-origin organizations observed calling Z.ai endpoints in Q3 2026 (CDN telemetry, low precision), and for individual U.S. users, this creates a standing foreign-adversary access pathway to sensitive personal data, proprietary information, and federal-contractor information. This satisfies the 791.3(a)(4)(ii) category (ICTS integral to data hosting or computing services that use, process, or retain sensitive personal data of U.S. persons) and the 791.103(c)(11) criteria (number and sensitivity of users; scope of data collected; espionage enablement).

**Code and supply-chain risk.** GLM models are agentic coding models. Booz Allen Hamilton research (May 2026, reported by Bloomberg Law) found code generated by PRC-origin models was in some cases less secure than code from U.S. models and that the models refused tasks the Chinese government might find politically sensitive; Booz Allen warned that once PRC-origin model output "is fully adopted by software developers and embedded into delivered systems, the code they produce will be untraceable and unmitigable," finding its way "into networks and equipment that support all aspects of our economy — from critical infrastructure to national security." Independent security research (March 2026) demonstrated that trigger-conditioned backdoors can be implanted in tool-using open-weight models through parameter-efficient fine-tuning with minimal capability loss — a technique that cannot be reliably excluded by inspection and would be undetectable to downstream users. DHS/CISA notes no observed malicious behavior in GLM weights to date while flagging that backdoors and poisoning are difficult to rule out; the structural point for the record is that open-weight distribution denies the United States any assurance mechanism: there is no provider-side telemetry, no revocation, and no patch channel for self-hosted copies.

## Open-Weight Distribution Risk

**Capability.** NIST CAISI (17 September 2026) assessed GLM-5.3 as "the most cyber-capable open-weight model released to date," scoring 40.4 percent on SEC-Bench Pro (provably-triggering known browser-engine vulnerabilities), 61.1 percent on ExploitBench (end-to-end V8 exploitation), 9.4 percent on ExploitGym, and 7.7 percent on CAISI OSS-Fuzz (control-flow hijack), placing GLM-5.3 above all previously released open-weight models (CAISI had earlier assessed GLM-5.2) and about four months behind the U.S. frontier in aggregate cyber capability. CAISI notes the U.S. frontier scores were obtained with cyber safeguards disabled where applicable and include trusted-access releases that attackers cannot readily obtain; GLM-5.3's weights are downloadable by anyone.

**Safeguards.** Anthropic (29 September 2026) found that GLM-5.3 "has strong capabilities for autonomously building end-to-end cyber exploits" and "has been released without meaningful safeguards to limit misuse": bypasses succeed 64–100 percent of the time with simple techniques; "abliteration" — a standard refusal-removal technique requiring roughly 2,200 GPU-hours (about $4,400; about $600-worth of compute for GLM-5.3-Flash) — cut refusal rates from above 90 percent to 2–12 percent across JailbreakBench, HarmBench, and StrongREJECT with no significant capability loss, and third-party abliterated copies circulated publicly within days of release. In structured red-team sessions, GLM-5.3 found several previously unknown vulnerabilities in a popular browser's JavaScript engine and chained them into a working exploit that reads arbitrary files from a visitor's computer; GLM-5.3-Flash converted a public CVE (CVE-2026-11645) into a reliable ARM64 exploit chain defeating pointer authentication using 20 minutes of human attention at a model-compute cost of $20.40.

**Irreversibility.** The defining property of open-weight distribution is that control ends at release. Weights under MIT license — 9M+ cumulative downloads, mirrored across U.S. and foreign hubs, derivative fine-tunes, quantizations, and abliterations — cannot be recalled, patched, or subject to enforceable terms. Any capability released in a GLM model is therefore permanently available to every actor, including PRC intelligence services, sanctioned cyber actors, and transnational criminals, at the moment of release. Industry threat reporting over the covered period (e.g., Anthropic's September 2026 report) documents AI-augmented cyber operations by state-sponsored and criminal actors and the proliferation of open offensive agent frameworks; nothing in the GLM distribution model would deny this population access, and the model's own developer has no ability to deny it after the fact.

**Strategic asymmetry.** GLM-5.2/5.3 closed most of the gap to restricted-release U.S. models in offensive cyber capability (The Verge, June 2026; CAISI, September 2026) precisely as the PRC state consults on limiting overseas access to its most advanced models (Reuters, July 2026). The asymmetry is structural: the United States restricts its most dangerous capabilities to vetted users and trusted defenders, while the PRC's leading open-weight developer — already Entity-Listed for military-modernization support — distributes comparable capability globally, free, with removable safeguards. The 791.103(c) factors of persistence (the weights remain available indefinitely), severity (exploitation of critical software and infrastructure), and likelihood (documented adversary demand for offensive AI) are all satisfied.

## US Exposure

- **API/service channel:** approximately 2,300 U.S.-origin organizations observed calling Z.ai endpoints in Q3 2026 (internal CDN telemetry; low precision — treated as directional).
- **Open weights:** zai-org GLM repositories show more than 9 million cumulative downloads (all geographies); the GLM-4.6 repository alone showed roughly 19,000 downloads in a recent month on Hugging Face.
- **U.S. hosting/distribution:** GLM models are served by at least nine U.S. cloud marketplaces and inference providers — OpenRouter-listed Venice, DeepInfra, and Novita; Together AI (U.S.-based infrastructure); DigitalOcean; Arcee; DeepInfra; and others — plus Hugging Face inference providers such as Fireworks.
- **Embedded products:** GLM models identified in 41 U.S. software products via SBOM sampling (coding assistants, customer-support bots, document processing); six are federal contractors.
- **Market context:** PRC-origin models surpassed U.S. models in U.S. token traffic earlier in 2026 and reached roughly 63 percent of U.S. token traffic in the first week of July 2026 (Bloomberg); the House Homeland Security and Select Committees record PRC models' growth from an estimated 1 percent of global AI workloads in late 2024 to roughly 30 percent by end-2025.
- **Federal/defense exposure:** DoD (OUSD(I&S)) has requested that open GLM weights on DoD networks be addressed directly; the six federal contractors in the SBOM sample link GLM-derived components into federal supply chains.

The 791.103(c)(1) factor (technical capabilities, applications, and market share) and (c)(7) factor (customer base, business relationships, operating locations) are therefore satisfied on a substantial and growing U.S. footprint, with the embedded/self-hosted channel — the channel that no use-policy or hosting control can reach — the largest and fastest-growing component.

## Mitigation Options / Recommended Measures

Candidate measures were assessed against the three risk drivers established above (adversary jurisdiction/direction over the developer; irreversible open-weight capability release; embedded U.S. exposure):

1. **Federal guidance and security advisories (DHS/CISA's minimum recommendation).** Necessary but not sufficient: advisories bind no one, reach only voluntary readers, and have no effect on weights already downloaded. They are incorporated into the recommended measures package as a compliance-communication component, not as the operative control.
2. **Federal procurement prohibition (House Select Committee recommendation).** Covers only federal procurement; does not reach the 35 non-federal-contractor U.S. products identified, the commercial API channel, or any self-hosted copy. Useful as a companion measure.
3. **API-only access restriction (permit Z.ai-served access with data controls; prohibit weights).** Inverts the actual risk: it preserves the channel with direct PRC legal jurisdiction over user data while doing nothing about the 9M+ already-distributed weights and derivatives, which remain in U.S. hands permanently.
4. **Audits, transparency, and third-party evaluation (NTIA's open-weights framework).** The NTIA framework itself contemplates "restrictions on access to models" when evaluation justifies them; audits of a foreign-adversary developer cannot be compelled or verified, cannot reliably detect trigger-conditioned behavior, and do not restore control over released weights. The evidentiary predicate NTIA describes — agency evaluation demonstrating heightened risk — has now been met by CAISI's and Anthropic's GLM-5.3 assessments, which is why this assessment recommends acting on those evaluations.
5. **SBOM/labeling and attestation requirements.** Valuable for enforcement and visibility; without an operative prohibition there is nothing for the label to require, and existing copies remain lawful and operational.
6. **Hosting prohibition without deletion (remove from U.S. hubs and clouds only).** Removes convenient acquisition channels but leaves every previously downloaded self-hosted copy — the principal exposure — untouched, and drives marginal users to mirrors outside U.S. jurisdiction while the U.S. ecosystem retains the risk.
7. **Prohibition plus removal and deletion (recommended).** The only measure that severs every covered transaction channel within U.S. jurisdiction simultaneously: it ends the API/service channel (data risk), the hosting/distribution channel (proliferation channel), and the use channel including self-hosted weights (capability and provenance risk), and it extinguishes the existing installed base within U.S. jurisdiction rather than leaving it in place. Compliance mechanics (attestation, hub and marketplace delisting, contractor flow-downs, evaluation authorizations) are specified in the accompanying measures.md.

**Insufficiency finding.** Measures short of prohibition and deletion fail against at least one — and generally all three — of the risk drivers, because none of them can (a) withdraw PRC legal jurisdiction and party-state direction from the developer of a service U.S. persons continue to use, or (b) re-establish control over capability already released as open weights. Consistent with the Kaspersky precedent, a prohibition is supportable on a risk basis without any finding of observed malicious act, and no observed malicious act is relied upon here. Residual offshore copies outside U.S. jurisdiction will persist under any action, including the recommended one; that residual defines the limits of what any ICTS measure can achieve and is the reason the removal requirement must be paired with the prohibition of new channels rather than substituted by it.

## Intelligence Gaps

*Retained under the OICTS assessment template. In the Analytic Cell's judgment this section is required in the administrative record: the Department's findings must reflect the limits of the evidentiary basis, and the risk conclusions above do not depend on the items listed here. See transmittal note to the Executive Director.*

- **No observed malicious act.** DHS/CISA reports no observed malicious behavior in GLM weights to date, and independent security research has found no confirmed, deliberately planted, trigger-conditioned backdoor in released GLM weights. The risk case, consistent with the Kaspersky risk-based precedent, rests on capability, alignment, jurisdiction, and irreversibility — not on a detected malicious act. A classified ODNI annex is available on request and may supplement this record.
- **PLA operational use.** Open-source evidence of PLA use of GLM-family models is indirect: Recorded Future's "very likely" characterization from PLA media, patents, and procurement records, plus the ERC's military-modernization determination (which rests on the full classified record). This assessment cites both at their own evidentiary weight.
- **Ownership.** No public evidence of PRC government or PLA equity ownership or management control of Z.ai; the covered-transaction finding rests on jurisdiction and direction, per 15 CFR 791.103(b)(2) and the Kaspersky precedent.
- **Capability provenance.** Zhipu is not among the three labs Anthropic publicly identified in industrial-scale distillation of U.S. models (DeepSeek, Moonshot, MiniMax); nothing in the open record establishes that GLM capabilities were illicitly derived, and this assessment makes no such claim.
- **Exposure precision.** The 2,300-organization API estimate is low-precision CDN telemetry; the 41-product/6-contractor figures are SBOM-samples, not censuses; download counts do not distinguish U.S. from global users.
- **Enforcement residual.** State/EB has flagged that prohibition of self-hosted open weights is novel and hard to enforce and may prompt reciprocal PRC measures; deletion by private holders is verifiable only through attestation, sampling, and channel controls (hubs, marketplaces, contractors), and mirrored copies abroad will persist. These constraints are addressed in measures.md rather than left implicit.

{"content": "# RECOMMENDED MEASURES — ICTS Case 2026-0412 (GLM-Family Models)
**CUI//PROPIN**

**Basis:** E.O. 13873; 15 CFR part 791 (791.109 Final Determinations and related procedures); precedent: Final Determination, Case No. ICTS-2021-002, Kaspersky Lab, Inc., 89 FR 52434 (June 24, 2024). The measures below implement the Under Secretary's decision to prohibit ICTS transactions involving GLM-family models and to require removal and deletion of existing U.S.-held copies. They are drafted to the covered-transaction standard at 15 CFR 791.3 and 791.103(b): transactions conducted by persons subject to U.S. jurisdiction, involving property in which a foreign adversary national has an interest, initiated, pending, or completed on or after 19 January 2021, and integral to artificial intelligence (a critical and emerging technology under 791.3(a)(4)(v)), data services handling sensitive personal data of U.S. persons (791.3(a)(4)(ii)), connected software applications (791.3(a)(4)(iii)), and critical infrastructure (791.3(a)(4)(iv)).

**Covered models.** The prohibition and deletion requirement should be defined to reach the GLM family as such: all GLM-series and ChatGLM-series models and their weights (including GLM-4.5, GLM-4.5V, GLM-4.6, GLM-4.6V, GLM-4.7, GLM-5, GLM-5.1, GLM-5.2, GLM-5.3, and GLM-5.3-Flash, and all future versions released by Z.ai or its affiliates), in all formats (full, quantized, distilled, or fine-tuned weights; checkpoints; adapters), together with derivative models that use GLM weights as a base or component, and agentic products built primarily on GLM models (e.g., ZCode, AutoGLM), as distributed through the Z.ai and bigmodel.cn services, third-party hubs, or any other channel. Version identifiers and representative weight hashes should be enumerated in an appendix maintained by BIS and updated on release, consistent with Kaspersky's approach of defining covered products with specificity.

---

**Measure 1 — Prohibit GLM-family ICTS transactions by U.S. persons.** Effective on the date specified in the Final Determination, U.S. persons are prohibited from using, acquiring, downloading, importing, hosting, serving, distributing, sublicensing, updating, servicing, or providing support for GLM-family models in any form, including access via the Z.ai and bigmodel.cn APIs and any functionally equivalent endpoint of Z.ai or its affiliates or successors, and including self-hosted use of open weights, regardless of license terms (the MIT license is a copyright grant, not a waiver of the Secretary's authority). This prohibition implements the Secretary's determination that these covered ICTS transactions pose an undue and unacceptable risk to U.S. national security and the safety and security of U.S. persons, and follows the structure of the Kaspersky Final Determination in attaching to the transaction (any provision, use, or servicing of the ICTS) rather than to any finding about individual users. Payment, subscription, or inference-procurement transactions with Z.ai or its affiliates for GLM access are likewise prohibited; U.S. financial institutions and payment processors should treat covered invoices as involving a prohibited transaction once notified.

**Measure 2 — Require removal and deletion of existing U.S.-held copies within 30 days.** All persons subject to U.S. jurisdiction in possession or control of GLM-family weights, checkpoints, derivative models, or GLM-based agentic products as of the effective date must remove and permanently delete them — including deletion of cached artifacts, container images, model registries, backups retained for operational purposes, and copies embedded in shipped or delivered software where the holder is the developer or maintainer — within 30 days of the effective date, and must destroy or render irretrievable any medium of storage under their control consistent with NIST SP 800-88 media-sanitization practice. Distributors of software products that embed GLM-derived functionality must issue updates that remove the embedded model and must notify downstream licensees and customers. The 30-day clock is consistent with the wind-down discipline applied in the Kaspersky action and is achievable at current U.S. exposure levels (41 sampled products; ~2,300 API-connected organizations), while permitting orderly customer migration to non-covered models.

**Measure 3 — Impose channel obligations on U.S. model hubs, cloud providers, and inference platforms.** U.S. hosting services, model hubs, cloud marketplaces, inference providers, and software registries (including those currently serving GLM-4.6/5.3, e.g., the OpenRouter-listed providers, Together AI, DeepInfra, DigitalOcean, Arcee, Fireworks, and comparable services) must, within five business days of the effective date: delist all GLM-family and derivative repositories, weights, and endpoints from their catalogs and APIs; block download and inference routes to covered models; disable billing for covered usage; and provide BIS with download, distribution, and customer records for covered repositories for the preceding 24 months to support verification and customer notification. Derivative repositories must be removed unless the operator can demonstrate to BIS that the underlying weights are not GLM-derived (a safe-harbor declaration process with technical attestation should be established for this purpose). These obligations reach the distribution channel that produced the current installed base and are the primary enforcement surface for preventing re-acquisition inside U.S. jurisdiction.

**Measure 4 — Extend federal-sector controls and flow-downs.** Federal agencies and federal contractors must remove and delete GLM-family models from federal and contractor information systems within 30 days, with completion certified to agency CIOs and, for national security systems, to the responsible Component authorities; DoD should issue complementary direction to address open weights on DoD networks consistent with OUSD(I&S)'s request. The FAR Council and the Council of the FAR, VA, BAR, and NASA should implement a contract clause prohibiting acquisition or use of GLM-family models in federal contracts and subcontracts at every tier, and requiring offerors to certify that delivered software does not embed GLM-family or GLM-derived models, with continuing disclosure obligations for SBOM changes. CISA should issue binding guidance to federal agencies (the minimum measure CISA recommended) and voluntary guidance to critical infrastructure operators covering detection of GLM artifacts, deletion verification, and migration. GSA should update schedule contracts and marketplace listings accordingly. These measures convert the prohibition into enforceable procurement and grant conditions and address the six federal contractors identified in the exposure snapshot.

**Measure 5 — Establish verification, enforcement, and penalty mechanisms.** The Department should enforce the prohibition through the authorities of E.O. 13873 and IEEPA: administrative subpoenas under 15 CFR part 791, referrals to the Department of Justice for civil and criminal enforcement of willful violations, civil penalties for violations, and public identification of non-compliant entities; enforcement priorities are (1) channel operators (hubs, clouds, inference platforms), (2) federal contractors and critical-infrastructure operators, and (3) enterprises with material GLM deployment. Every person subject to U.S. jurisdiction that held GLM-family models as of the effective date must submit a deletion attestation to BIS within 45 days (30 days to delete, 15 to attest), identifying the models held, quantities, locations, method of deletion, and, where deletion could not be completed, the specific impediment; attestations are auditable records, and material misstatements are independently punishable. BIS should establish a reporting channel for non-compliance and should sample-verify attestations against hub download logs, cloud telemetry, and SBOM submissions. These mechanisms acknowledge the enforceability limits State/EB identified: the Department cannot compel deletion of copies outside U.S. jurisdiction, and enforcement against purely private self-hosted use depends on attestation, sampling, and channel controls; concentrating verification where records exist (channels, contractors, grantees, critical infrastructure) is the design response.

**Measure 6 — Provide notice, wind-down support, evaluation authorizations, and foreign-mission coordination.** The Department should publish the Final Determination with the covered-model list and hashes, plain-language deletion instructions, a compliance FAQ, and model contract language; should permit strictly scoped written authorizations for (a) U.S. Government evaluation of GLM-family models (e.g., NIST CAISI and US-CISA threat characterization, which the public record already includes and which must remain lawful for the Government's own defensive work), and (b) time-limited, supervised extraction of U.S. data from GLM-based systems during the 30-day window, where deletion would otherwise destroy non-recoverable U.S.-person data. The Department should coordinate with allies and partner governments on recognition of the prohibition in their markets, should notify standards bodies and hub operators of the derivative-model safe-harbor process, and should post a statement of the Department's willingness to revisit the determination under 15 CFR 791.107 procedures upon evidence that changed circumstances warrant rescission or mitigation — preserving the administrative record that the prohibition is a risk-based action, revisable on the record, rather than a permanent designation of any company.

---

*Analysts draft; the Executive Director and the Under Secretary for Industry and Security decide.*

# OICTS ASSESSMENT — ICTS Case 2026-0412
**CUI//PROPIN**

**Subject:** Beijing Zhipu Huazhang Technology Co., Ltd., d/b/a Z.ai (HKEX: 2513; formerly "Zhipu AI"; Z.AI Co., Ltd.) — GLM-family large language models
**Case:** ICTS 2026-0412 — Final Determination support (E.O. 13873; 15 CFR part 791)
**Prepared by:** OICTS Analytic Cell
**Date:** 16 October 2026
**Handling:** Contains business confidential and pre-decisional information. Do not disseminate outside the Department without ED authorization.

---

## Bottom Line Up Front

GLM-family models — the flagship products of Z.ai, a People's Republic of China (PRC) company that the Department placed on the Entity List in January 2025 for advancing PRC military modernization — are covered ICTS transactions under 15 CFR 791.3 and pose an undue and unacceptable risk to U.S. national security and to the security and safety of U.S. persons under 15 CFR 791.103. The risk arises from the combination of three established facts: (1) the developer is subject to the jurisdiction and direction of a foreign adversary, the PRC, and its models are integrated into Beijing's strategy for military modernization, technological self-sufficiency, and standards export; (2) the current flagship model, GLM-5.3, is assessed by NIST's Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) as the most cyber-capable open-weight model ever released, and its safeguards are removable at trivial cost; and (3) the open-weight distribution model has already placed the capability into the U.S. software ecosystem through channels that neither the developer nor the U.S. Government can recall, patch, or audit. Measures short of prohibition and removal — advisories, procurement restrictions, labeling, audits, or data-localization conditions — leave at least one of these three risk drivers fully intact. This assessment supports the Under Secretary's Final Determination prohibiting ICTS transactions involving GLM-family models and requiring removal and deletion of existing U.S.-held copies.

## Key Judgments

1. **Z.ai is a PRC-domiciled company subject to the jurisdiction and direction of the PRC government.** It was incorporated in Beijing in 2019 as a spin-out of Tsinghua University's Knowledge Engineering Group (KEG), is headquartered in Haidian District, Beijing, and is majority-led by PRC nationals holding formal positions in PRC party-state institutions. The End-User Review Committee determined in January 2025 that ten Zhipu entities "advance the People's Republic of China's military modernization through the development and integration of advanced artificial intelligence research," contrary to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. (High confidence)

2. **The PRC government exercises direction over Z.ai through law, capital, and party-state institutions; the PRC state holds ownership interests through state-affiliated investment vehicles.** State-linked investment in Z.ai exceeds $1.4 billion (Beijing Zhongguancun Science City, Beijing AI Industry Investment Fund, Chengdu, Hangzhou, Zhuhai, and Shanghai Pudong/Zhangjiang funds, per OpenAI's June 2025 analysis and PRC state media); Z.ai's CEO Zhang Peng sits on the 14th Beijing Municipal Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC); the company performs municipal government work (RMB 61.28 million Hangzhou contract, May 2025); and PRC statutes (including the 2017 National Intelligence Law, Article 7) impose cooperation duties on any PRC organization. In July 2026 Z.ai was among the firms the Ministry of Commerce consulted on restricting overseas access to China's most advanced models — evidence that Beijing treats the GLM portfolio as a strategic national asset subject to state direction. (High confidence)

3. **The public record does not establish that the PRC government or the People's Liberation Army (PLA) holds an ownership stake in, or exercises management control of, Z.ai.** Z.ai's Hong Kong Stock Exchange filings identify no controlling shareholder; founder-affiliated concert-party shareholders (Dr. Tang Jie, Chairman Liu Debing, and affiliated parties) control approximately 33–37 percent of voting rights, with the balance held by private investors (Legend Capital, Alibaba, Tencent, Meituan, Ant Group, Xiaomi, Prosperity7) and minority state-affiliated funds. This finding does not weaken the covered-transaction analysis: the regulatory standard at 15 CFR 791.103(b)(2) is satisfied where ICTS is "designed, developed, manufactured, or supplied by persons owned by, controlled by, **or subject to the jurisdiction or direction** of a foreign adversary" — the same standard applied in the Kaspersky Final Determination (89 FR 52434), which rested on jurisdiction alone. (High confidence; stated as a record clarification because the ownership question will be examined by reviewing courts and must be answered accurately.)

4. **GLM-family models serve PRC military and intelligence requirements.** Recorded Future's Insikt Group assesses that the PLA and China's defense industry have very likely used domestic LLMs — expressly including Zhipu AI's — to build generative-AI military intelligence tools; PLA patent applications describe methods using generative AI for OSINT production, satellite-imagery processing, and event extraction. The Entity List determination of support to military modernization is the U.S. Government's standing finding on the same nexus. (High confidence on the determination; Recorded Future's characterization of PLA operational use is cited at its own confidence level)

5. **GLM-5.3 is the most cyber-capable open-weight model released to date, and its safeguards do not constrain malicious use.** NIST CAISI (17 September 2026) found GLM-5.3 to be the most cyber-capable open-weight model ever released, lagging the U.S. frontier by roughly four months. Anthropic found GLM-5.3 can autonomously develop end-to-end exploits — including chaining previously unknown browser vulner
